Matthew.author: The Gospel does not name its author, but the ancient church held it was the apostle Matthew, also called Levi, the tax collector (Matthew 9:9) [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]]. Only this Gospel calls Matthew a tax collector, and it shows a writer who knew about coins and taxes [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].
Matthew.date: Most scholars place it before Jerusalem fell in AD 70, since 24:15 speaks of the temple as still standing. Irenaeus said Matthew wrote while Peter and Paul were in Rome, which would mean the 60s [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].
Matthew.to: Greek-speaking Jewish Christians, perhaps in Antioch in Syria, surrounded by neighbours hostile to the claims about Jesus. Matthew shows that Jesus is the Messiah Israel was waiting for [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].
Matthew.why: The Gospel of fulfilment. Jesus is the long-promised King, the son of David and son of Abraham [[bible:Matthew 1:1]], and in him the kingdom of heaven has come near [[bible:Matthew 4:17]] [[ks:25]]. Together with Mark, Luke and John it gives the foundational witness to Jesus’ life, teaching, death and resurrection [[cm:Matthew]].
Matthew.story: It bridges the two Testaments, showing again and again that Jesus fulfils what the prophets promised [[ks:25]]. It ends with the risen King sending his followers to make disciples of all nations [[bible:Matthew 28:18-20]], the blessing promised to Abraham reaching the whole world [[ks:25]].
Matthew.genre: A Gospel: the story of Jesus’ life, teaching, death and resurrection, with his teaching gathered into five great sections, such as the Sermon on the Mount (5–7) [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].
Matthew.debate: Whether Matthew or Mark was written first, and so which one drew on the other [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]]; this is part of the wider question of why Matthew, Mark and Luke are so alike in some places and different in others [[tbd:019:Synoptic Gospels]].

Mark.author: John Mark (Acts 12:12), a disciple of Peter. Papias, writing early in the second century, passed on that “Mark became Peter’s interpreter and wrote down accurately… all that he remembered” of the Lord’s words and deeds [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]].
Mark.date: Most scholars date it in the 60s [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]]. An early tradition says Mark wrote in Italy after Peter’s death in the mid-60s, though an earlier date cannot be ruled out [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]].
Mark.to: Probably Christians in Rome. It explains Jewish customs (7:3–4) and speaks to believers suffering persecution, perhaps under Nero from AD 64 [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]].
Mark.why: The good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God [[bible:Mark 1:1]], told at a run. The King has come, with power over sickness, demons and storms, yet he came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many [[bible:Mark 10:45]] [[ks:26]].
Mark.story: In Jesus the kingdom has come, hidden at first like a tiny seed [[bible:Mark 4:30-32]] [[ks:26]]. The turning point is Peter’s confession that Jesus is the Christ, and the book ends at an empty tomb [[bible:Mark 8:29]] [[bible:Mark 16:6]]. Mark was probably the first to write a Gospel, and by telling the story so plainly as history it ties Christian faith to real events in a real place [[cm:Mark]].
Mark.genre: A Gospel, not meant as a strict chronological biography [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]]. Its climax may be the Roman centurion’s words at the cross: “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (15:39) [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]].
Mark.debate: How the Gospel ends: two of the oldest manuscripts stop at 16:8 [[tosn:Mark 16:9-20]], and some think Mark meant to leave readers in awe at the empty tomb [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]]. Also whether Mark was the first Gospel written [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].

Luke.author: Luke the physician, Paul’s companion (Colossians 4:14). The Gospel does not name him, but the “we” passages in Acts, his second volume, place its writer with Paul, which points to Luke [[tbd:012:Luke, Gospel of]].
Luke.date: Debated. Some date it after AD 70; others before Paul’s death about AD 64, which would explain why Acts ends with Paul still in prison in Rome [[tbd:012:Luke, Gospel of]].
Luke.to: Theophilus, a reader who knew the wider Greco-Roman world better than the geography of Israel; Luke avoids terms a Gentile might find puzzling [[tbd:012:Luke, Gospel of]].
Luke.why: A careful, orderly account of Jesus [[bible:Luke 1:3-4]], the Saviour who came to seek and to save the lost [[bible:Luke 19:10]]. Luke shows God’s kingdom welcoming the poor, outsiders, women and sinners [[ks:27]]. Everything happens because God is working out a plan he set long ago: Jesus “must” preach, suffer, die and rise [[cm:Luke]] [[bible:Luke 24:7]].
Luke.story: Luke is the first half of a two-part work; Acts continues the story [[bible:Acts 1:1-2]]. The risen Jesus shows that all of Scripture, from Moses to the Prophets and Psalms, speaks of him [[bible:Luke 24:44-47]] [[ks:27]].
Luke.genre: A Gospel, opening with a preface on Luke’s careful research among eyewitnesses [[bible:Luke 1:1-4]].
Luke.debate: When it was written [[tbd:012:Luke, Gospel of]], its relationship to Matthew and Mark [[tbd:019:Synoptic Gospels]], and how the census “when Quirinius was governor of Syria” (2:2) fits what is known of Quirinius, who supervised a census of Judea in AD 6 [[tbd:017:Quirinius]].

John.author: The Gospel says it was written by “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (21:20, 24), and the evidence points most probably to the apostle John [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]]. The writer knew Jewish customs and the places of Jesus’ day well, and his account bears the stamp of an eyewitness [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]].
John.date: Long dated to the last decade of the first century; many now argue for a date before AD 70, since John speaks of the pool of Bethesda as still there (5:2) [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]].
John.to: Believers and seekers alike: “these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” [[bible:John 20:31]].
John.why: Written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name [[bible:John 20:31]]. The Word who was with God and was God became flesh and lived among us [[bible:John 1:1]] [[bible:John 1:14]] [[ks:28]].
John.story: Jesus is the true temple, the bread of life, the light of the world and the good shepherd: everything the Old Testament pointed to finds its fulfilment in him [[ks:28]]. He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world [[bible:John 1:29]]. Telling the same story from another angle, John adds depth to the picture of Jesus the other Gospels give [[cm:John]].
John.genre: A Gospel, with much that is not found in the other three [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]].
structure: The last evening with the disciples
John.debate: When it was written, and how it relates to the other three Gospels; the likeness may come from shared oral tradition rather than from John using them [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]]. Also the story of the woman caught in adultery, which is missing from the earliest manuscripts [[tosn:John 7:53-8:11]].

Acts.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul, who also wrote the Gospel; the “we” passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16) show the writer travelling with Paul [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]].
Acts.date: Debated: many say about AD 85; some date it to the early 60s, while Paul was imprisoned in Rome, since it does not tell of his trial [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]].
Acts.to: “Most excellent Theophilus”, a title of respect often used for Roman officials [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]] [[bible:Luke 1:3]].
Acts.why: The risen Jesus pours out his Spirit, and his followers carry the good news from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth [[bible:Acts 1:8]]. The kingdom spreads through the Spirit, prayer and the preaching of Jesus [[ks:27]]. Without it we would know nothing of Pentecost, Stephen, the first church in Jerusalem or how the good news first reached the Gentiles [[cm:Acts]].
Acts.story: Acts links the Gospels and the letters. The blessing promised to Abraham for every family on earth begins to reach the nations [[bible:Acts 3:25-26]] [[ks:27]], and the book ends with Paul in Rome, still proclaiming the kingdom of God [[bible:Acts 28:31]].
Acts.genre: The second volume of Luke’s account, telling how the message about Jesus spread from Jerusalem to Rome (1:8) [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]].
structure: Paul’s first journey and the council
Paul’s trials and voyage to Rome
Acts.debate: When it was written, and whether Theophilus was one person or stands for Christians in general [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]].

Romans.author: Paul, as scholars of every viewpoint agree [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]]. Tertius wrote it down for him (16:22) [[bible:Romans 16:22]].
Romans.date: Shortly before Paul took the collection to Jerusalem, around AD 57–58, while he was in Corinth [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]].
Romans.to: The Christians in Rome (1:7), Jews and Gentiles, a church Paul had not yet visited. Phoebe probably carried the letter [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]].
Romans.why: Paul’s fullest explanation of the good news. All have sinned [[bible:Romans 3:23]], and God makes people right with himself as a free gift through faith in Jesus [[bible:Romans 3:24]] [[ks:29]]. Its one great theme is the gospel, and it is less tied to its own time than almost any other New Testament book, so it speaks very directly to readers today [[cm:Romans]].
Romans.story: God keeps his promise to Abraham, who will inherit the world [[bible:Romans 4:13]] [[ks:29]]. By the Spirit, believers share in a new creation that will one day set all creation free [[bible:Romans 8:19-21]], and nothing can separate them from God’s love [[bible:Romans 8:38-39]]. It also shows how the Old Testament and the New, Israel and the church, belong together in one plan of God [[cm:Romans]] [[bible:Romans 11:25-26]].
Romans.genre: Paul’s most detailed letter, both a careful teaching document and a heartfelt personal letter [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]].
structure: New life in Christ and the Spirit
Romans.debate: What Paul means by “the righteousness of God” and how Jews and Gentiles alike are made right with God through faith [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]]; and where the closing praise belongs, after 14:23 or at the end of chapter 16 [[tosn:Romans 16:25-27]].

1 Corinthians.author: Paul, as scholars agree, with Sosthenes [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Corinthians]] [[bible:1 Corinthians 1:1]].
1 Corinthians.date: About AD 55, from Ephesus, during Paul’s third missionary journey [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Corinthians]].
1 Corinthians.to: The church in Corinth, a busy Roman port city and capital of Achaia, divided into groups and influenced by the pagan city around it [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Corinthians]].
1 Corinthians.why: Paul writes to a gifted but divided church and brings everything back to Christ crucified [[bible:1 Corinthians 2:2]]: their quarrels, their bodies, their worship and their gifts [[ks:29]]. It shows the unchanging gospel being applied to everyday problems in a real church [[cm:1-2 Corinthians]].
1 Corinthians.story: It holds the great chapter on love [[bible:1 Corinthians 13:4-7]] and the earliest written list of witnesses to the risen Jesus [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:3-8]]. Christ’s resurrection is the first fruits of ours [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:20]], and he reigns until every enemy, even death, is defeated [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:25-26]] [[ks:29]].
1 Corinthians.genre: A pastoral letter answering reports from Chloe’s household and the letter the Corinthians had sent Paul with their questions (7:1) [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Corinthians]].
structure: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross
1 Corinthians.debate: Head coverings in worship: Paul calls them a long-standing church custom, which most modern interpreters see as based on culture [[tosn:1 Corinthians 11:16]]; and the place of speaking in tongues, which the Corinthians prized too highly [[tosn:1 Corinthians 12:1-14:40]].

2 Corinthians.author: Paul, as is widely accepted [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.date: About AD 56, after Paul left Ephesus and travelled north to Macedonia [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.to: The church in Corinth, after a painful visit and a “letter of tears” that has been lost [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.why: Paul’s most personal letter. God’s power is made perfect in weakness [[bible:2 Corinthians 12:9]], and his treasure is carried in clay jars [[bible:2 Corinthians 4:7]] [[ks:29]]. No letter shows more of Paul the man and the pastor [[cm:1-2 Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.story: Paul serves the new covenant of the Spirit [[bible:2 Corinthians 3:6]]. Anyone in Christ is a new creation, and God has given us the ministry of reconciliation [[bible:2 Corinthians 5:17-18]] [[ks:29]].
2 Corinthians.genre: A deeply personal letter: Paul repairs his relationship with the church and restarts the collection for Jerusalem [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.debate: Whether 2:14–7:4 and chapters 10–13 were once separate letters, and whether 6:14–7:1 belongs where it is [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]] [[tosn:2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1]].

Galatians.author: Paul (1:1), once a devoted Jew who had attacked the church [[tbd:012:Letter to the Galatians]].
Galatians.date: It depends on where the churches were: an earlier date if Paul wrote to the churches he founded in southern Galatia on his first journey, a later one if to northern Galatia [[tbd:012:Letter to the Galatians]].
Galatians.to: The churches of Galatia, in what is now Turkey, troubled by Jewish Christians who taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved [[tbd:012:Letter to the Galatians]].
Galatians.why: Paul’s passionate letter about freedom in Christ. We are made right with God by faith in Jesus, not by keeping the law, and Gentiles belong to God’s family by faith [[bible:Galatians 2:16]] [[ks:29]]. Its importance is out of all proportion to its size, because people always drift toward thinking salvation is their own achievement [[cm:Galatians]].
Galatians.story: Christ is the promised offspring of Abraham, so all who belong to Christ are Abraham’s heirs [[bible:Galatians 3:16]] [[bible:Galatians 3:29]] [[ks:29]]. The Spirit produces new life, and its fruit is love, joy and peace [[bible:Galatians 5:22-23]].
Galatians.genre: A sharp, urgent letter that skips Paul’s usual thanksgiving and goes straight to a rebuke [[tosn:Galatians 1:1-5]].
structure: Faith and the promise to Abraham
Galatians.debate: Whether Paul wrote to northern or southern Galatia, which affects its date [[tbd:012:Letter to the Galatians]].

Ephesians.author: Paul names himself (1:1; 3:1), and early Christian writers such as Irenaeus, Polycarp and Ignatius accepted it as his. Some features lead many scholars to doubt this, though they make sense if the letter was meant for several churches [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]].
Ephesians.date: From prison (3:1; 6:20); most scholars think from Rome, between about AD 59 and 63 [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]].
Ephesians.to: The Christians in Ephesus and the nearby churches; there are no personal greetings, which fits a letter meant for several congregations [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]].
Ephesians.why: God’s plan to bring all things together under Christ [[bible:Ephesians 1:9-10]]. We are saved by grace through faith [[bible:Ephesians 2:8]], and Jews and Gentiles become one new people [[ks:29]].
Ephesians.story: The church is God’s new temple, a dwelling for God by the Spirit [[bible:Ephesians 2:21-22]] [[ks:29]]. The letter then shows how that new life looks at home, at work and in spiritual battle [[bible:Ephesians 6:10-11]]. From first to last it is God who plans and gives salvation, and Christ himself is our peace [[cm:Ephesians]] [[bible:Ephesians 2:14]].
Ephesians.genre: A letter whose purpose is praise: it opens like a hymn, “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:3), and grounds its teaching on how to live in its teaching about God [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]].
Ephesians.debate: Whether Paul wrote it, and whether it was meant for Ephesus alone [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]]; and how the household instructions (5:21–6:9) apply, beginning with the call to all to submit to one another [[tosn:Ephesians 5:22]].

Philippians.author: Paul, with Timothy named at the start, though Timothy probably acted as his secretary [[tbd:016:Philippians, Letter to the]].
Philippians.date: From prison (1:12–13). Rome around AD 62 is most likely; others suggest Ephesus around AD 55 or Caesarea around AD 58 [[tbd:016:Philippians, Letter to the]].
Philippians.to: The church in Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia, who had sent Paul a gift by Epaphroditus [[tbd:016:Philippians, Letter to the]].
Philippians.why: A letter of joy written from prison [[bible:Philippians 1:13]]. At its heart is Christ, who humbled himself to death on a cross and was raised to the highest place [[bible:Philippians 2:6-11]] [[ks:29]]. It is a rare letter to a church Paul is well pleased with, full of thanks for their partnership [[cm:Philippians]] [[bible:Philippians 1:3-5]].
Philippians.story: Every knee will bow and confess that Jesus Christ is Lord [[bible:Philippians 2:10-11]]. Believers already belong to heaven and wait for their Saviour to come [[bible:Philippians 3:20-21]] [[ks:29]].
Philippians.genre: A warm letter of thanks and encouragement, with an early Christian hymn about Christ at its centre (2:6–11) [[tosn:Philippians 2:6-11]].
Philippians.debate: Where Paul was imprisoned when he wrote it: Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea [[tbd:016:Philippians, Letter to the]].

Colossians.author: Paul, with Timothy. The tradition is well established, but many scholars today question it because of its theology and style [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]].
Colossians.date: It depends on where Paul was imprisoned: if in Rome, as long held, between AD 60 and 62; more scholars now suggest Ephesus, earlier [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]].
Colossians.to: The church in Colossae, which had been taught by Epaphras (1:7) and was threatened by a false teaching [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]].
Colossians.why: Christ is supreme. He is the image of the invisible God, and all things were made through him and for him [[bible:Colossians 1:15-16]], so believers need nothing added to him [[ks:29]]. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [[bible:Colossians 2:3]] [[cm:Colossians]].
Colossians.story: God has rescued us from darkness and brought us into the kingdom of his beloved Son [[bible:Colossians 1:13]]. On the cross Christ triumphed over every hostile power [[bible:Colossians 2:15]] [[ks:29]].
Colossians.genre: A letter answering false teaching by making clear who Christ is, built on the hymn of 1:15–20 [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]] [[tosn:Colossians 1:15-20]].
Colossians.debate: What the false teaching in Colossae was, since Paul never clearly defines it, and who wrote the letter [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]].

1 Thessalonians.author: Paul, with Silas (Silvanus) and Timothy; phrases like “I, Paul” (2:18) show that Paul mainly wrote it. The few scholars who doubt this lack strong evidence [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Thessalonians]].
1 Thessalonians.date: Probably early in AD 50, from Corinth, about a year after Paul first preached in Thessalonica [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Thessalonians]].
1 Thessalonians.to: “The assembly of the Thessalonians” (1:1), a young church in Macedonia that Paul had been forced to leave, facing persecution [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Thessalonians]].
1 Thessalonians.why: Encouragement for a young church facing hardship: keep growing in faith, love and hope [[bible:1 Thessalonians 1:3]] [[ks:29]]. It holds Paul’s fullest teaching on what will happen when Jesus returns [[cm:Thessalonians]].
1 Thessalonians.story: Those who have died in Christ are not lost: when the Lord comes, the dead in Christ will rise first, and we will always be with the Lord [[bible:1 Thessalonians 4:16-17]] [[ks:29]].
1 Thessalonians.genre: A pastoral letter written after Timothy’s good report, praising their faith and answering their questions [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Thessalonians]].
structure: Living to please God and the Lord’s coming
1 Thessalonians.debate: What 4:13–18 teaches about Christ’s return. Paul wrote it to comfort the grieving: all who belong to Jesus will live with him for ever [[bsn:1 Thessalonians 4:13-18]] [[tosn:1 Thessalonians 4:14]].

2 Thessalonians.author: Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy, signed in his own hand (3:17). Some scholars doubt it because it speaks of the future differently from 1 Thessalonians [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.date: Not stated. Most likely soon after 1 Thessalonians, since Silas and Timothy were still with Paul [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.to: “The assembly of the Thessalonians”, still suffering and confused about the day of the Lord [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.why: A follow-up for a church shaken by false rumours: the day of the Lord has not yet come, so stand firm and keep working [[bible:2 Thessalonians 2:1-3]] [[ks:29]]. Together with 1 Thessalonians it is a main source of the New Testament’s teaching on the last things [[cm:Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.story: When Jesus returns he will put right every wrong and be glorified in his people [[bible:2 Thessalonians 1:7-10]]. Until then the Lord is faithful to strengthen and guard them [[bible:2 Thessalonians 3:3]] [[ks:29]].
2 Thessalonians.genre: A short pastoral letter: stand firm and hold to what you were taught (2:15) [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.debate: Authorship and order of the two letters [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]], and who or what is restraining the man of lawlessness (2:6–7) [[tosn:2 Thessalonians 2:6]].

1 Timothy.author: Paul is named in the first verse, and early church tradition from Irenaeus (about AD 185) links only his name with it; its many personal references to Paul’s life are strong evidence. Some scholars argue against it from its vocabulary, which differs from his other letters [[tbd:020:Timothy, First Letter to]].
1 Timothy.date: If Paul wrote it, after his first release from prison in Rome, around AD 61 or 62, and before his second imprisonment [[tbd:020:Timothy, First Letter to]].
1 Timothy.to: Timothy, whom Paul had left in charge of the church in Ephesus (1:3) [[tbd:020:Timothy, First Letter to]].
1 Timothy.why: Paul guides his young co-worker in caring for a church. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners [[bible:1 Timothy 1:15]], so the church must hold to that truth and live it out [[ks:29]]. Paul writes as a father to a trusted son in the faith [[cm:1 Timothy]] [[bible:1 Timothy 1:2]].
1 Timothy.story: There is one God and one mediator between God and people, Christ Jesus [[bible:1 Timothy 2:5]]. The church is the household of God, the pillar and foundation of the truth [[bible:1 Timothy 3:15]].
1 Timothy.genre: One of the three “Pastoral Letters”, grouped together since the second century: advice on church order, leaders and false teaching [[tbd:016:Pastoral Letters]].
1 Timothy.debate: Who wrote the Pastoral Letters [[tbd:020:Timothy, First Letter to]], and how 2:11–15 on women teaching should be understood [[tosn:1 Timothy 2:12]].

2 Timothy.author: Paul. Even many who doubt he wrote the Pastoral Letters accept that 2 Timothy has genuine parts from him, and the evidence for his authorship is stronger than against it [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].
2 Timothy.date: Between AD 64 and 67, from prison in Rome, shortly before Paul was martyred under Nero [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].
2 Timothy.to: Timothy in Ephesus [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].
2 Timothy.why: Paul’s last letter, written as he faces death. Guard the good news, endure hardship, and preach the word [[bible:2 Timothy 4:2]] [[ks:29]]. Written in the shadow of execution, it shows how a Christian can face death calmly and faithfully [[cm:2 Timothy]].
2 Timothy.story: Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching [[bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]. Paul has fought the good fight and looks to the crown the Lord will give to all who love his appearing [[bible:2 Timothy 4:7-8]] [[ks:29]].
2 Timothy.genre: A kind of last will and testament from the apostle [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].
2 Timothy.debate: Authorship, as with the other Pastoral Letters [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].

Titus.author: Paul (1:1). Modern scholars question this because of its language and style, but many respected scholars defend it [[tbd:020:Titus, Letter to]].
Titus.date: Hard to date: probably after Paul’s release from his first imprisonment in Rome, when many believe he worked in Crete and Greece [[tbd:020:Titus, Letter to]].
Titus.to: Titus, a Gentile convert and one of Paul’s most trusted co-workers, left in Crete to continue the work (1:5) [[tbd:020:Titus, Letter to]].
Titus.why: Appoint good leaders and teach a way of life that fits the good news, because God’s grace has appeared, bringing salvation [[bible:Titus 2:11-12]] [[ks:29]].
Titus.story: God saved us not by our works but by his mercy, through the new birth the Spirit gives [[bible:Titus 3:5]]. We wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ [[bible:Titus 2:13]]. Set among the rough people of Crete, it shows that the good news is for the most unlikely people and changes how they live [[cm:Titus]] [[bible:Titus 1:12]].
Titus.genre: A Pastoral Letter: advice on church order, leaders and false teaching [[tbd:016:Pastoral Letters]].
Titus.debate: Authorship, with the other Pastoral Letters [[tbd:020:Titus, Letter to]].

Philemon.author: Paul, writing as a prisoner for Christ (1:9) [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]].
Philemon.date: From prison, probably in Ephesus or Rome, at the same time as Colossians (compare Colossians 4:7–14) [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]].
Philemon.to: Philemon, a church leader in Colossae who had come to faith through Paul, with Apphia, Archippus and the church in his home [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]].
Philemon.why: A short, personal letter. Paul asks Philemon to welcome back Onesimus, a runaway slave who has become a Christian, no longer as a slave but as a dear brother [[bible:Philemon 1:16]] [[ks:29]]. Paul could have commanded, but he appeals out of love and leaves the choice to Philemon [[cm:Philemon]] [[bible:Philemon 1:8-9]].
Philemon.story: It shows the good news at work in one household: in Christ, people divided by the world become one family [[bible:Galatians 3:28]] [[ks:29]].
Philemon.genre: A short personal appeal, though addressed to many people, not only Philemon [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]].
Philemon.debate: What exactly Paul asks of Philemon; one view is that he wants Onesimus freed and welcomed as a full member of the family [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]] [[bible:Philemon 1:16]].

Hebrews.author: Not stated. Some early writers held that Paul wrote it, but its anonymity and its writer’s learning from eyewitnesses (2:3) argue against this. Barnabas was an early suggestion; Luther first proposed Apollos [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]].
Hebrews.date: Probably before AD 70, since it says nothing of the temple’s destruction and speaks as if sacrifices were still offered; perhaps AD 67–70 [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]].
Hebrews.to: Jewish Christians, as its early title “To Hebrews” suggests, who had suffered for their faith and were tempted to turn back [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]].
Hebrews.why: Jesus is greater than angels, greater than Moses and greater than every priest, and his one sacrifice brings full forgiveness [[bible:Hebrews 10:12-14]]. So hold on to him in faith [[ks:30]].
Hebrews.story: Hebrews shows how the Old Testament’s priests, sacrifices and covenant point to Christ, the priest-king who brings the new covenant [[bible:Hebrews 8:6]] [[ks:30]]. Like Abraham, believers look for the city God has prepared [[bible:Hebrews 11:16]] and receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken [[bible:Hebrews 12:28]]. It also teaches us how to read the Old Testament, as one long story whose people, places and practices point to Christ [[cm:Hebrews]].
Hebrews.genre: “The word of exhortation” (13:22), showing that Christ is far greater than Judaism’s greatest heroes [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]].
structure: The new covenant and one sacrifice
Hebrews.debate: Who wrote it [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]], and the warning passages such as 6:4–8, among the most challenging in the New Testament [[tosn:Hebrews 6:4-8]].

James.author: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Most scholars identify him as James the brother of Jesus; James the son of Zebedee was killed in AD 44 [[tbd:012:Letter of James]].
James.date: Many scholars believe it was written early, possibly AD 45–49, when many Jewish Christians had not yet fully separated from Judaism [[tbd:012:Letter of James]].
James.to: “The twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (1:1): Jewish Christians facing trials [[tbd:012:Letter of James]].
James.why: Practical wisdom for followers of Jesus. Real faith shows itself in action [[bible:James 2:17]]: in how we speak, how we treat the poor, and how we trust God in trials [[ks:31]]. Its chief warning is against being double-minded, trying to have the best of this world and the next [[cm:James]] [[bible:James 1:8]].
James.story: James has been called the Proverbs of the New Testament, and it echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount [[ks:31]]. Believers live under King Jesus now and wait patiently for his coming [[bible:James 5:7-8]] [[ks:31]].
James.genre: Practical wisdom for the first generation of Christians, written like an Old Testament prophet and full of proverbs [[tbd:012:Letter of James]].
structure: The tongue and wisdom from above
James.debate: How 2:14–26 fits with Paul on faith; James may be correcting a misunderstanding of Paul’s teaching on justification by faith [[tbd:012:Letter of James]] [[tosn:James 2:24]].

1 Peter.author: The apostle Peter (1:1), a witness of Christ’s sufferings (5:1). Silas (Silvanus) helped him write it (5:12), perhaps as his secretary or translator. Some scholars think its Greek too good for a fisherman and that someone else wrote in his name; others disagree [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]].
1 Peter.date: Probably AD 64 or 65, from Rome, called “Babylon” in 5:13 [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]].
1 Peter.to: Believers, many of them Gentiles, scattered across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, in what is now Turkey [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]].
1 Peter.why: Hope for Christians who suffer as outsiders. God has given them a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection [[bible:1 Peter 1:3]], so they can live well and follow Christ’s example [[ks:32]]. Its great theme is hope: suffering lasts only a little while, then comes glory [[cm:1 Peter]] [[bible:1 Peter 5:10]].
1 Peter.story: The church is God’s chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation [[bible:1 Peter 2:9]], a living temple built on Christ [[ks:32]]. Suffering comes first, then glory, as it did for Jesus [[bible:1 Peter 5:10]] [[ks:32]].
1 Peter.genre: A letter much concerned with suffering, echoing more of Jesus’ words than almost any other New Testament letter [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]].
1 Peter.debate: Authorship [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]], and the meaning of Christ preaching to “the spirits in prison” (3:19) [[tosn:1 Peter 3:19-20]].

2 Peter.author: Simon Peter (1:1). Its style differs from 1 Peter, so a trusted co-worker may have gathered Peter’s final concerns [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].
2 Peter.date: Probably in Rome, after AD 60 and before AD 70; Peter was martyred about AD 64 [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].
2 Peter.to: Perhaps the same churches as 1 Peter (3:1), endangered by teachers promoting immorality [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].
2 Peter.why: Peter’s farewell: grow in the knowledge of Jesus, trust the Scriptures, and do not doubt that the Lord will return [[bible:2 Peter 1:19-21]] [[ks:33]]. It shows how wrong belief, such as denying that Jesus will return, quickly leads to wrong living [[cm:2 Peter]].
2 Peter.story: The Lord is not slow but patient, wanting all to come to repentance [[bible:2 Peter 3:9]]. We look for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells [[bible:2 Peter 3:13]] [[ks:33]].
2 Peter.genre: Peter’s final words, a kind of testament for the church [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].
2 Peter.debate: Who wrote it, and its close relationship to Jude, a shortened form of which appears in chapter 2 [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].

1 John.author: Traditionally the apostle John. It shares so much vocabulary, style and thought with the Gospel of John that the two are closely connected, and its opening claims an eyewitness (1:1) [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
1 John.date: Probably near the end of the first century [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
1 John.to: John’s “children”, churches threatened by false teaching [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
1 John.why: A letter so that believers may know they have eternal life [[bible:1 John 5:13]]. Walk in the light, love one another, and believe that Jesus came in the flesh [[ks:28]].
1 John.story: God is love [[bible:1 John 4:8]], and he showed it by sending his Son to atone for our sins [[bible:1 John 4:10]] [[ks:28]]. It helps believers tell real faith from counterfeit, so that they can rest in God’s assurance [[cm:Johannine Epistles]].
1 John.genre: A simple but deep answer to false teaching, setting the true way beside the false [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
1 John.debate: Whether “the elder John” Papias mentions was a different person from the apostle [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]]; and the words added to 5:7–8 in a few late manuscripts [[tosn:1 John 5:7-8]].

2 John.author: “The elder” [[tbd:019:Second Letter of John]], traditionally John [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
2 John.date: In a setting much like 1 John [[tbd:019:Second Letter of John]].
2 John.to: “The chosen lady and her children”, probably a church and its members [[tbd:019:Second Letter of John]].
2 John.why: A short note to a church: walk in truth and love, and do not welcome teachers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh [[bible:2 John 1:6-7]] [[ks:28]].
2 John.story: A companion to 1 John, holding truth and love together [[bible:2 John 1:3]] [[ks:28]].
2 John.genre: A brief letter warning a church not to welcome false teachers [[tbd:019:Second Letter of John]].
2 John.debate: Whether the lady is a woman or a church [[tosn:2 John 1:1]].

3 John.author: “The elder”, writing in a setting like the other letters of John [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].
3 John.date: In a setting like 1 and 2 John [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].
3 John.to: Gaius, who stayed loyal to the elder [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].
3 John.why: A personal letter praising Gaius for welcoming travelling Christian workers, and warning about Diotrephes, a leader who loved to be first [[bible:3 John 1:5-9]] [[ks:28]].
3 John.story: A glimpse of everyday life in an early house church, and of how love for one another shows itself in practice [[bible:3 John 1:11]] [[ks:28]].
3 John.genre: A short personal letter asking Gaius to care for travelling missionaries [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].
3 John.debate: The conflict with Diotrephes, who rejected the elder’s authority [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].

Jude.author: “Jude… brother of James” (1:1), understood by many as Jude the brother of Jesus [[tbd:010:Jude, Letter of]].
Jude.date: Not stated; probably between AD 60 and 100 [[tbd:010:Jude, Letter of]].
Jude.to: Churches troubled by false teachers [[tbd:010:Jude, Letter of]].
Jude.why: Contend for the faith once delivered to the saints [[bible:Jude 1:3]], stay in God’s love, and wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus [[bible:Jude 1:21]] [[ks:33]]. It reminds every generation that attractive but false teaching will come, and that the truth is worth guarding [[cm:Jude]].
Jude.story: It ends with one of the Bible’s great blessings, praising God who is able to keep us from stumbling [[bible:Jude 1:24-25]] [[ks:33]].
Jude.genre: A short letter urging believers “to contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints” [[bible:Jude 1:3]].
Jude.debate: Its quotations from books outside the Bible, the Assumption of Moses and 1 Enoch (1:14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9), and what kind of false teaching it opposed [[tbd:010:Jude, Letter of]].

Revelation.author: John (1:9). The earliest sources say the apostle John, son of Zebedee; Dionysius of Alexandria first questioned this because of its style [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
Revelation.date: Either shortly after Nero (AD 54–68), or near the end of Domitian’s reign (AD 81–96), as Irenaeus said [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
Revelation.to: Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, now western Turkey; John wrote from Patmos, where he was likely exiled for his faith [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
Revelation.why: Visions that pull back the curtain on history. The Lamb who was slain has won the victory [[bible:Revelation 5:5-6]], evil will be judged, and God will make all things new [[bible:Revelation 21:5]] [[ks:34]]. No book shows God’s sovereignty more vividly, and the conquering rider is always the Lamb who was slain [[cm:Revelation]].
Revelation.story: The last book completes the story that began in Genesis. The ancient serpent is defeated [[bible:Revelation 12:9-11]], the whole renewed creation becomes God’s dwelling, and his people will see his face [[bible:Revelation 22:3-4]] [[ks:34]].
Revelation.genre: Apocalyptic prophecy in the form of a letter: “in spirit and inner purpose, a pastoral”, as H. B. Swete put it [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
structure: The risen Christ and letters to seven churches
The end and the new creation
Revelation.debate: How to read chapters 4–22: as about the future (futurist), the course of history (historicist), events of John’s own time (preterist), or a symbolic message (idealist) [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
